ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) is a rapid, specific test that uses fluorescent-labeled antibodies to detect viral or bacterial antigens in patient specimens. It is especially useful when quick diagnosis is needed, such as in suspected viral conjunctivitis or rabies exposure.

sections.p: DFA uses fluorescently labeled antibodies that bind directly to antigens in a specimen. The bound complex is visualized under a fluorescence microscope, allowing immediate confirmation of infection.
The test targets viral or bacterial proteins expressed on the surface of infected cells or in secretions. Common targets include adenovirus in conjunctivitis or rabies virus in brain tissue.
Not applicable to the test itself; DFA is used after specimen collection. For rabies, transmission is via bites; for adenovirus, via droplets or contact.
DFA is used to diagnose infections such as viral conjunctivitis, measles, rabies, and certain bacterial infections like pertussis. It is not a disease.
Specimen types vary: conjunctival swab for adenovirus, skin biopsy for rabies, vesicle scraping for herpes. The sample is incubated with fluorescent-labeled antibodies, then examined.

t.b: Positive fluorescence indicates presence of antigen; negative suggests absence or low levels.
Positive culture supports DFA; negative may be due to low viral load.
Positive PCR confirms infection; useful when DFA unavailable or inconclusive.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe or worsening symptoms of suspected rabies exposure; rapidly progressing conjunctivitis with vision loss; high fever with rash and lymphadenopathy in children.

faq.q: What if the DFA result is negative but clinical suspicion is high?
faq.a: Repeat the test with a fresh specimen or use PCR; consider other etiologies.

faq.q: Can DFA be used in low-resource settings?
faq.a: Yes, if a fluorescence microscope is available; otherwise, rely on clinical judgment and alternative tests.

faq.q: Is DFA safe for the clinician?
faq.a: Standard biosafety precautions apply; the test uses fixed specimens, so risk is low.

exam: Explain how DFA provides rapid diagnosis in viral conjunctivitis and why it is preferred over culture.
Describe the specimen collection and interpretation steps for a DFA test for rabies.
Discuss the limitations of DFA and when PCR should be used instead.
